system.name: LS S4/S5 The past in the present

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Historical context: Ancient societies existed a very long time ago and they look different to the societies we have today. We can learn about ancient societies through stories, artefacts or sites.

This focus area aligns with:

  • Stage 4 Historical context 1 (core): The ancient past
  • Stage 4 Depth studies: The ancient past

The following ancient societies can be explored in this focus area. Teachers can choose to focus on one or more of these societies:

  • Ancient Egypt 
  • Ancient India 
  • Ancient China 
  • Ancient Greece 
  • Ancient Rome 

Content in Working with historical concepts and skills outlines how historical concepts and skills are to be integrated with all other content in this focus area as part of the process of historical inquiry.

system.name: LS S4/S5 The ancient world: ancient societies

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Historical context: In the medieval world many societies had hierarchies (feudalism) and religion was the source of knowledge and authority. Forces such as conquests, innovation, trade or disease led to change in the medieval world.

This focus area aligns with:

  • Stage 4 Historical context 2 (core): The medieval world
  • Stage 4 Depth studies: The medieval world

The following societies can be explored in this focus area. Teachers can choose to focus on one or more of these societies:

  • Medieval Europe (c. 590 – c. 1600) 
  • The expansion of Islam (c. 610–1258) 
  • Polynesian expansion across the Pacific (c. 700–1756) 
  • The Vikings (c. 790–1066) 
  • The Angkor/Khmer Empire (c. 802 – c. 1431)  
  • Japan under the Shoguns (c. 794–1867) 
  • Mongol expansion (c. 1206–1368) 
  • The Ottoman Empire (c. 1299 – c. 1683) 
  • The Black Death in Asia, Europe and North Africa (c. 1347 – c. 1351) 
  • Renaissance Italy (c. 1400 – c. 1600) 
  • The Spanish conquest of the Americas (c. 1492 – c. 1572)

Organisation of History 7–10

Figure 1 shows the organisation of History 7–10.

The History focus areas consist of Historical context studies and Depth studies.

Image long description: In Stage 4, 3 focus areas are listed under the heading ‘Historical contexts (core)’. The focus areas, The ancient past Historical context (core) and The medieval world Historical context (core) are linked to a box under the heading ‘Depth studies (options)’. The box is labelled ‘Depth study (select at least 2 from 16 options). The third focus area under the heading ‘Historical contexts (core)’ in Stage 4, The era of colonisation, is linked to the Depth study (core): Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation. A line surrounds the Stage 4 focus areas, the Depth studies (core) and Depth studies (options), and links to 2 boxes labelled ‘1 case study’ and ‘1 site study’. In Stage 5, 2 focus areas are listed under the heading ‘Historical contexts (core)’. The focus area, The making of the modern world is linked to 2 Depth studies (core): Australia: making a nation from Federation to WWI and Australia at war – WWII. The second focus area, The modern world is linked to the Depth study (core) Human rights and freedoms. The 3 Depth studies (core) are linked to a box under the heading ‘Depth studies (options)’. The box is labelled ‘Depth study (select at least 1 from 10 options)’. A line surrounds the Stage 5 focus areas, the Depth studies (core) and Depth studies (options), and links to 2 boxes labelled ‘1 case study’ and ‘1 site study’. The focus areas for Stage 4 and Stage 5 are encircled by a line labelled ‘Historical concepts’ at the top of the diagram and ‘Historical skills’ underneath the diagram representing integration as part of the historical inquiry process.

Life Skills outcomes and content

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

Creating written texts supports learning

The development of the History 7–10 Syllabus follows Recommendation 2: ‘Clarify and strengthen writing content in syllabus documents’ from Teaching Writing: Report of the Thematic Review of Writing (NESA 2018).

Creating written texts facilitates learning as it promotes explicitness, encourages the integration of ideas, supports reflection, fosters personal engagement and aids learners to think about the significance and implication of ideas. Each subject has particular and specific writing demands relevant for communicating within and about the discipline. Writing about content enhances understanding across subjects and stages.

The secondary curriculum includes:

  • systematic development of expectations for creating written texts which align with the English K–10 Syllabus (2022)
  • explicit writing content to support students to become fluent creators of texts and to deepen their understanding of the subject area
  • opportunities to practise the process of creating written texts to develop and communicate knowledge, understanding and ideas
  • a focus on development of word consciousness and precise use of subject-specific terminology.

Creating written texts refers to the act of composing and constructing a text for a particular purpose, audience and context.

Various methods of transcription may be employed, and a student’s preferred communication form(s) should be considered when teaching.

Balance of content

The outcomes describe the knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of teaching and learning. Teachers should use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content included in each focus area.

The amount of content associated with a given outcome is not necessarily indicative of the amount of time spent engaging with the respective outcome. Teachers use formative and summative assessment to determine instructional priorities and the time needed for students to demonstrate expected outcomes.

In considering the intended learning, teachers make decisions about the sequence and emphasis to be given to particular groups of content based on the needs and abilities of their students.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Courses

The History 7–10 Syllabus includes 2 courses:

  • History
  • History Life Skills

Focus of learning

History develops in students an interest in and enjoyment of exploring the past. A study of History provides opportunities for students to develop historical knowledge through a critical understanding of themselves and others in the continuum of human experience. Opportunities to foster historical thinking by cultivating historical inquiry skills and encouraging participation in society as active, informed and responsible citizens are a feature throughout the History 7–10 Syllabus.

What students learn

Students develop knowledge and understanding about the actions and lived experiences of people over time. They learn to apply the skills of historical inquiry by making connections, constructing coherent accounts and explanations of the past and deepening their knowledge and understanding of History. Students learn to analyse sources as evidence and to sequence major historical periods to show an understanding of historical concepts including continuity and change, cause and effect, perspectives, significance and contestability. They develop historical skills in comprehension, analysis and use of sources, perspectives and interpretations, research and communication to construct logical historical arguments supported by relevant evidence and communicating effectively about the past for different audiences and different purposes.

In Years 7–8, students learn about the ancient past, the medieval world and the era of colonisation in overarching chronological historical context studies. Students have the opportunity to deepen their understanding of these periods via the depth study options and the core depth study Aboriginal Peoples Experiences of Colonisation in Australia.

In Years 9–10, students learn about the making of the modern world and the modern world in overarching chronological historical context studies. Students have the opportunity to deepen their understanding of these periods via the depth study options and the core depth studies of Australia: Making an Australia – from Federation to WWI, Australia at War – WWII and Human rights and freedoms.

Case studies and site studies are used to extend students' knowledge and understanding.

Case studies

Case studies are a detailed exploration or analysis of a significant group, individual, idea, belief, practice or event related to one or more focus areas. Case studies assist students to understand how an event, individual, place or idea fits into a broader historical narrative and connects to historical themes, processes and trends.

Site studies

Site studies can be undertaken in person or virtually. Site studies are an examination of a historically significant location related to a focus area. Site studies allow students to engage in research and analysis to gain deeper historical insights. Students gain historical skills in source analysis, interpretation of physical evidence and drawing connections between historical context and physical sites.

Examples of case studies and site studies are provided in the teaching advice.

Course requirements

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the History 7–10 Syllabus.

Stage 4

In Stage 4 (100 hours) students are required to complete:

  • 3 core historical context studies – The ancient past, The medieval world, and The era of colonisation
  • ONE core depth study – Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation
  • at least 2 other depth studies options (3 options can be chosen overall in Stage 4)
  • ONE case study (one topic of choice aligned to any of the focus areas in Stage 4 – approximately 5 hours)
  • ONE site study (one topic of choice aligned to any of the focus areas in Stages 4 – approximately 5 hours)

At least ONE depth study option in either Stage 4 or 5 is to be chosen from a non-western option (marked with an *).

Stage 5

In Stage 5 (100 hours) students are required to complete:

  • 2 core historical context studies – The making of the modern world, and The modern world
  • 3 core depth studies – Australia: making a nation – from Federation to WWI, Australia at war – WWII, and Human rights and freedoms

Life Skills

For History Life Skills 7–10:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more History Life Skills 7–10 outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the History Life Skills 7–10 outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • Case studies and site studies are an essential part of the study of History. Where appropriate, students should have the opportunity to undertake case or site studies to develop their understanding and demonstrate achievement of History Life Skills 7–10 outcomes.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students with disability can access the syllabus outcomes and content in a range of ways. Decisions regarding curriculum options should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Some students with intellectual disability may find the Years 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content the most appropriate option to follow in Stage 4 and/or Stage 5. Before determining whether a student is eligible to undertake a course based on Life Skills outcomes and content, consideration should be given to other ways of assisting the student to engage with the Stage 4 and/or Stage 5 outcomes, or prior stage outcomes if appropriate. This assistance may include a range of adjustments to teaching, learning and assessment activities.

Life Skills outcomes cannot be taught in combination with other outcomes from the same subject. Teachers select specific Life Skills outcomes to teach based on the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of each student. Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Life Skills outcomes.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Students explore their interests and preferences, building self-awareness, and engage with groups with similar interests through community access. They explore a range of perspectives on popular culture and demonstrate openness to the ideas of others.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope to learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about the impact of advances in technology in changing one form of popular culture, the outcome requires them to sequence events in chronological order. Students explore advances in technology related to music, arranging the use of vinyl records, CDs, MP3s and digital streaming licences into different time periods.

Making connections

Content from the Backgrounds, origins and connections to popular culture in Australia content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to popular culture in Australia

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Powerhouse Museum locations, Sydney
  • Case study: Music events across the decades
  • Case study: Iconic TV shows

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – similarities and differences in an aspect of popular culture from the post-Second World War (WWII) era to the present day
  • cause and effect – the impact of technology on Australian lifestyle and popular culture
  • perspective – how multiculturalism has enriched popular culture
  • Significance – influence of an international music act on popular culture in Australia

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Popular culture in Australia (1945 – c. 2010): Background, origins and connections to popular culture in Australia

Individual preferences for entertainment, sport, fashion, literature or art

Historical skills: Research

  • use digital technologies to locate and access information
Students select an area of interest within popular culture and use digital technology to locate and access information. For example, students may select fashion that was popular from the 1950s to today. They may engage with sources showcasing fashion styles from different decades. Students identify their preferred styles within various eras.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What were the social forces that impacted the generation of teenagers in the 1950s?
  • How did music, movies, TV, fashion, technology, books and magazines shape teenagers globally from the 1950s to 2010?
  • Who were the cultural icons from the 1950s to 2010 and why?
  • How have cultural icons from the 1950s to the 1980s continued to influence contemporary cultural icons?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • The increasing influence of American culture on Australians in the 1950s


Students studying Stage 5 content research components of American culture in the 1950s, considering fashion, music, movies, car design and lifestyle choices. They identify the relationships of these American culture components to Australian culture and the implications for Australian life. Students choose one area of interest and create a flow chart outlining the impact.

Life Skills:

  • The role of a key individual in shaping popular culture
Students studying Life Skills content explore American cultural icons from the 1950s related to an area of interest such as music, movies, politics, transport or fashion. They create a collage showcasing the icon that they have selected.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Historical concepts are integral to the development of historical understanding. Knowledge and understanding, concepts and skills are interrelated and should be taught in an integrated way to provide meaningful learning experiences for students.

The historical concepts are used to investigate and understand the past. One or more historical concept can be addressed in each focus area. The selected historical concept(s) should align with the content and enable students to view and engage with the world through a particular lens.

system.name: LS S4/5 Teaching advice for Historical concepts

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Historical skills support the development of historical understandings that enable students to make sense of the past. They work in conjunction with historical concepts. Historical skills are required to engage in historical inquiry and should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

Teachers should explicitly teach students how to communicate historical information, recognising students’ preferred communication form(s). Students need to be taught key vocabulary used to describe the past. Teachers should encourage EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when learning key vocabulary.

system.name: LS S4/5 Teaching advice for Historical skills

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Through historical inquiry, students make connections with the past and deepen their knowledge and understanding of history. The stages of historical inquiry include:

Historical inquiry is an active process which involves asking questions, gathering evidence, interpreting sources and communicating ideas or understanding about people, events or societies from the past. Students may engage in all or part of the inquiry process. When selecting sources for historical inquiry, teachers consider the accessibility of the source, including readability levels of written materials, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions for videos, and tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Students have opportunities to develop their understanding of equity, individual rights and responsibilities to support self-advocacy. They consider concepts of self-determination when exploring the rights and freedoms of Aboriginal Peoples. Students also encounter a range of perspectives and may develop skills in negotiating or being open to the ideas of others particularly when engaging with case studies and historical inquiry.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about key aspects of Aboriginal Peoples’ fight for land rights, the outcome requires them to identify aspects of Aboriginal Peoples’ struggle for rights and freedoms. Students may engage with sources and stories about Aboriginal People’s relationships with Land and Country and name difficulties and conflicts related to land rights.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to human rights and freedoms content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to human rights and freedoms.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: the Aboriginal Tent Embassy – its origins and enduring protest
  • Case study: Eddie Koiki Mabo, a leader for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  • Case study: Dunghutti Elders Council – first land claim in NSW
  • Case study: Charles Perkins and the 1965 Freedom Ride

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – changes to laws regarding human rights
  • cause and effect – how the fight for rights and freedoms affected Aboriginal Peoples
  • significance – the 1967 referendum
  • contestability – debates on the success of land rights legislation.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activity

Human rights and freedoms (c. 1938 – c. 2017): Significant groups, individuals, ideas, beliefs, practices or events in human rights and freedoms

  • Experiences of children who were part of the Stolen Generations

Historical skills: Research

  • ask who, what, where, when, why and how questions about person(s) who lived in the past, a past event, place, object or story
Students engage with information about the Stolen Generations. They are supported with verbal and visual prompts to develop questions about the experiences of children who were part of the Stolen Generations.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • How were the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples different to the rights of other groups and individuals in society?
  • Who were the significant individuals or groups who supported the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?
  • What rights and freedoms have women needed to fight for?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • The purpose and influence of human rights conventions
Students studying Stage 5 content conduct research into human rights conventions and explore their purpose and influence, nationally and globally. They curate a collection of images that explain the significance and impact of the conventions.

Life Skills:

  • Key components in the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)


Students studying Life Skills content safely access sources and locate information about the UDHR. They identify one human right from the UDHR and demonstrate their understanding by selecting a collection of images or audio recordings that represent this right.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Students develop skills using and interpreting data and information as they explore where, how and why people came to Australia. They learn about others in the community and strategies to overcome challenges by learning about the experiences of people coming to Australia. Students celebrate diversity when engaging with case studies and historical inquiry related to multiculturalism.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are participating in school or local activities or events that promote intercultural understanding, the outcome requires them to demonstrate understanding of civic participation. They participate in local school or community activities that promote intercultural understanding, such as Harmony Week.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to Migration experiences content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to Migration experiences.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Case study: Personal or local migration stories
  • Case study: A diary, movie or documentary about the migrant experience
  • Case study: Migration experience from one country
  • Case study: Anh Do’s experience of migration

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

  • continuity and change – similarities and differences in migrant journeys to Australia in the 1970s and the present day
  • cause and effect – the introduction of the multiculturalism policy in Australia
  • perspective – migrant groups’ contributions to Australia
  • significance – the significance of a global event on a group migrating to Australia.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Migration experiences (1945 – c. 2016): Background, origins and connections to migration experiences

  • Reasons people migrate

Historical skills: Perspectives and interpretations

  • recognise that other people have a variety of perspectives on events
Students are supported to identify reasons why people leave their home and travel to new and unfamiliar lands. The teacher guides students to conduct a think-pair-share about reasons they might move to live in another place. Additionally, they seek reasons of a family member or familiar person, to recognise reasons people migrate.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • Why did people migrate to Australia after 1945?
  • Which groups of people migrated to Australia from 1945?
  • What was Australia’s response to these waves of migration?
  • How have migrants helped shape contemporary Australia?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • The contribution of migrants to Australia’s social, cultural and economic development and changing identity as a multicultural society
Students studying Stage 5 content engage with texts, media reports and/or oral histories that describe the contributions of migrants to Australia. They individually or collaboratively present their findings about the social, cultural and economic impacts to their peers or a broader audience in celebration of Australia's multicultural society.

Life Skills:

  • Aspects of everyday life that are influenced by culture


Students studying Life Skills content identify examples of culture in everyday life and the contribution of culture to language, technology, health, food, fashion, art or sport. They share these examples with their peers or a broader audience in celebration of Australia's multicultural society.

content.value:
Purpose

Students develop their understanding of the rights and freedoms of Australian women and engage in advocacy around social issues. They have opportunities to learn how equity for women can impact agency and independence.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are learning about the similarities and differences between the lives of women prior to the Second World War (WWII) and women today, the outcome requires students to recognise continuity and change. Students are presented with images of women that represent daily living before WWII and today. They recognise what has stayed the same and what has changed using gestures, eye gaze or verbal responses.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to Rights and freedoms of Australian women content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the rights and freedoms of Australian women.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Case study: South Australian suffragettes
  • Case study: Oodgeroo Noonuccal
  • Case study: International Women’s Day

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • cause and effect – the impact of WWII on women’s role in the home, local community and government
  • perspective – differing views on the role of women across social groups
  • significance – the role of a significant woman in the fight for rights and freedoms
  • contestability – debates on the need for laws to protect women.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Rights and freedoms of Australian women (c. 1945 – c. 2012): Background, origins and connections to rights and freedoms of Australian women

  • Women in a range of fields, nationally and globally

Historical skills: Analysis and use of sources

  • locate information in a source
Students are presented with a range of written, digital and visual sources related to women in national and global fields. They are supported with visual and verbal prompts to identify information about women conducting various activities or jobs in each source.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What role did women play in the workforce before 1960?
  • How do the rights of women in Australia compare to those in another country?
  • What rights have Australian women had to fight for?
  • What rights do women still fight for in contemporary Australia?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • Role of at least ONE significant individual in the fight for the rights and freedoms of women after WWII



Students studying Stage 5 content engage with sources about an individual who has played a significant role in the fight for the rights and freedoms of women after WWII. They collect evidence about why and how that individual has made a difference, considering the specific cause that they upheld. Students explain to peers the significance of this individual.

Life Skills:

  • The role of a key individual or group in the women’s rights movement
Students studying Life Skills content are provided with resources and supported to select facts about the role of a key individual or group involved in the women’s rights movement. They draw conclusions about how they effected change and share details with peers.

Purpose

Teachers can develop a school-developed option that considers the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students. This provides opportunities for students to engage with historical people, places and events of personal interest and relevance.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are: Focus of study, Consider site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills, Consider historical inquiry processes, and Select the content.

Focus of study

Select an option, choose outcomes and define the focus.

For example:

  • Ancient Australia – Songlines and stories
  • Women in ancient and medieval times – Rulers, queens, warriors and maids
  • Experiences of migrants in Australia – Stories from local communities
  • Australia and the Vietnam War – commemoration and remembrance
  • Sport and the Australian Story – Sporting legends
  • Rights of people with disability – The history of the Paralympics
  • Technological change and development in 20th and 21st centuries – Telephones, transport and technology.

Consider a site study or case study

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Adventurers of Antarctica
  • Case study: Symbols and styles – Fashion from ancient and medieval times
  • Case study: Tilly Aston’s fight for rights for people who are blind in Australia

Consider historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

Select historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

Consider historical inquiry process

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills.

For example:

  • What were the primary causes of this event or development?
  • Why is the individual or event considered significant in history?
  • In what ways did the social, political or economic structures change over time?
  • How did different groups perceive this specific event or development?

Select content

Select content from the syllabus as appropriate to the outcomes, focus of study, site or case study, student learning needs and school context, considering:

  • backgrounds and origins
  • significant groups, individuals, ideas, beliefs, practices or events
  • impact and legacies.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Considerations may include:

  • scaffolds and supports for conducting research and participating in a collaborative inquiry
  • participating in part or whole of a historical inquiry
  • students communicating their learning using their preferred communication form(s)
  • encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when discussing ideas and planning for writing.

Connecting with Stage 4 and Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content integrated with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

When selecting an option, consider one that enables the engagement of all students. For example, when engaging with a school-developed option about women in ancient and medieval times, students studying Life Skills content could locate sources to answer questions about the past, while students studying Stage 5 content could identify, locate, select and organise information from a variety of sources, including digital technologies and other methods.

Purpose

Students explore sustainability and ways to care for the environment to build community engagement and responsible citizenship. They develop decision-making and problem-solving skills as they explore environmental impacts on sites.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are exploring local activities or events that care for the environment, the outcome requires students to identify ways to engage with local and national issues. Students may focus on waste and recognise and name ways they can participate in local activities to reduce waste.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to The environmental movement content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the environmental movement.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: A local area impacted by environmental change
  • Site study: Machu Picchu, Peru
  • Case study: Aboriginal ways of caring for Country
  • Case study: Earth Day

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

  • continuity and change – changes in environmental movements from 1960 to today
  • cause and effect – the impact of protests on popular views of environmental issues
  • perspective – the need for environmental protection of specific regions or species
  • significance – the impact of an individual or group on public views about the environment.

Historical skills

Historical skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

The environmental movement (c. 1960 – c. 2015): Background, origins and connections to the environmental movement

  • A site that has been impacted by environmental change

Historical skills: Communication

  • communicate ideas about people, events or societies
Students explore images of a site that has been impacted by environmental change. Sites could include Port Arthur, Rapa Nui and Venice. They communicate ideas about environmental change by gesturing to, pointing to or naming key features that have changed.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • Why should the environment be protected?
  • How have issues have been addressed by the environmental movement?
  • Which groups have protected the environment in Australia and what have they achieved?
  • What is Australia’s role in environmental protection in Australia and globally?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • Impact of at least ONE event on changing attitudes to the environment such as, Tasmania Dams Case (1983, Commonwealth v Tasmania), the sinking of Greenpeace’s Rainbow Warrior (1985), Chernobyl disaster (1986), Jabiluka mine controversy (1998), Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill (2010)

Students studying Stage 5 content engage with videos, images and reports of the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill (2010). They investigate responses to the spill from individuals, the media, and environmental, industry and political groups. Students explain how the event led to new attitudes and movements focused on reducing dependency on fossil fuels and promoting sustainable practices.


Life Skills:

  • A significant event, development or campaign that contributed to popular awareness of an environmental issue
Students studying Life Skills content engage with videos, images and reports of the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill (2010). They explore how beaches wildlife were affected by the spill. Students explore the ongoing clean-up efforts and initiatives to restore the affected areas and protect the environment and may engage in community access to participate in similar clean-up activities of a local or familiar site.

content.value:
Content focus

The Migration experiences depth study focuses on enhancing students’ historical knowledge and skills through an immersive study of this period in history. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a case study or site study.

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area:

Historical context 5 (core): The modern world

  • The origin and significance of the United Nations Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including Australia’s involvement
  • Rise of movements for civil, political, social, cultural and economic rights in Australia and globally
  • The contribution of migrants to Australia post-World War II

Key ideas

  • Patterns of migration and diaspora following the Second World War
  • From the White Australia policy to multiculturalism policy
  • Reasons that people migrated to Australia
  • International law to which Australia is signatory, such as The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol
  • Experiences of migrants and refugees
  • Contributions of migrants and refugees to Australian society

Key terms

  • assimilation 
  • asylum seeker 
  • diaspora
  • humanitarian program
  • immigration 
  • migrant
  • multiculturalism 
  • persecution
  • refugee 
  • resettlement
  • skilled migration

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – Australian migration policies, changing demographics and diaspora of cultural groups
  • Cause and effect – international conflicts, including the Vietnam War and Australia’s response
  • Perspectives – migrants driving innovation, entrepreneurship and contributions to economic growth
  • Significance – introduction of the multiculturalism policy
  • Contestability – use of language involving asylum seekers and refugees.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline of key migration events between 1945 and 2016
  • collating and comparing migration statistics between the 1940s and 2010s
  • analysing sources such as Prime Minister Ben Chifley’s 1949 speech on post-war reconstruction and migration
  • locating and selecting sources depicting migrants’ contributions to major works such as the Snowy Mountains Scheme
  • researching key migration events and policy implementation in Australia such as implementation and disbanding of the White Australia policy, the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), the Federal Government’s 1983 Humanitarian Program, the Pacific Solution, and the implementation of offshore processing  
  • analysing a range of sources, including photographs, film sources, personal accounts, media reports and government documents to examine the role and impact of the Federal Government policy on migration patterns in Australia.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • How did the Australian Government response through the ‘populate or perish’ policy influence the size and composition of Australia’s population?
  • How did the White Australia policy affect migration to Australia and what were the reasons for its abolishment?
  • What were the major shifts in Australia’s immigration policy from the 1970s onward?
  • What were the experiences and challenges faced by migrants and refugees during their journey to Australia, with a focus on one specific group that arrived since 1945? 
  • How have migrants and refugees contributed to Australia’s social, cultural and economic development?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to develop deep knowledge and understanding of an aspect of migration experiences and the opportunity to acquire, process and communicate historical information. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Assisted Passage Migration Scheme
  • Greek Australians: cafes and milk bars
  • Post-WWII migration: building Australia’s workforce and infrastructure
  • The Tampa affair (2001)
  • Tu Do (‘freedom’) arrival in Darwin Harbour (1977)
  • National Maritime Museum, Sydney
  • National Museum of Australia, Canberra
  • State Library of New South Wales Archives, Sydney
  • Immigration Museum, Melbourne

Considerations for teaching and learning 

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support and, where appropriate, use their home language or dialect when exploring sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by analysing a range of impacts on migration to Australia post-WWII such as economic impacts, cultural integration of migrants or ethics of immigration policies.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

The purpose of this historical context study is to develop historical knowledge related to the modern world. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a depth study, case study or site study.

The focus of this context study is an exploration of the decades following the Second World War. The focus area includes the core depth study of Human rights and freedoms, and depth study options include Rights and freedoms of Australian women, Migration experiences, Popular culture in Australia, and The environmental movement.  

Building knowledge

This context study builds on the content covered in the historical context study 4 (core) The making of the modern world and depth study options. The period following the Second World War saw the formation of the United Nations and increased awareness of human rights and sustainability issues. The period is characterised by The Cold War and decolonisation as well as economic growth, immigration, social change, new technologies and shifts in popular culture.

Key ideas

  • Significance of the formation of the United Nations and its foundational documents in promoting human rights
  • Influence of the Cold War on societal attitudes and popular culture
  • Struggle and achievements of civil, political, social, cultural and economic rights
  • Civil rights and women’s liberation movements
  • Post-WWII diaspora and contribution of migrants to Australia
  • Growing international awareness of the environmental movement

Key terms

  • affirmative action
  • civil liberties
  • civil rights movement
  • communism
  • counterculture
  • decolonisation
  • economic justice
  • equal pay
  • Iron Curtain
  • nuclear arms race
  • social justice
  • sustainability
  • United Nations
  • United Nations Charter
  • universal suffrage

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – migration patterns and movements between 1940 and 2010
  • Cause and effect – consequences of ideological differences and territorial disputes emerging from the Cold War
  • Perspectives – portrayals of the Cold War in literature, film and music
  • Significance – role of Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) in fostering a collective understanding of human rights
  • Contestability – effectiveness of civil rights movements in improving the lives of disadvantaged people and promoting equity.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline of the key events from The Cold War
  • creating a presentation on the roles of the different UN bodies
  • discussing the key articles in the UDHR and examining Australia’s contributions to the UN
  • selecting sources such as government documents, archival materials, media reports, books, artefacts, audiovisual sources, photographs and interviews and recording the types of propaganda used during the Cold War
  • researching a major technological innovation that influenced society, such as transistors, computers, mobile phones, internet
  • creating an annotated photo essay with examples of the successes of civil, political, social, cultural and economic rights movements.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry: 

  • What were the differences between the United Nations and the League of Nations?
  • In what ways did the Cold War shape global politics and influence popular culture?
  • What mechanisms have different groups, including women, used in the struggle for rights and freedoms?
  • In what ways have migrants contributed to and shaped Australian society and culture since WWII?
  • How have technological advancements since WWII driven changes in society?
  • What are the drivers of the growing awareness of environmental issues?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Nelson Mandela and South Africa
  • The fall of the Berlin Wall
  • The nuclear arms race
  • The Space Race
  • National Museum of Australia, Canberra
  • The Berlin Wall Memorial, Germany
  • The National Civil Rights Museum, USA
  • United Nations Headquarters, USA

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by debating how key events from 1945 onwards have shaped international relations and global governance.

Purpose

Students develop understanding about Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences and perspectives of the past and build empathy as they consider the impact of colonisation. By building knowledge about Aboriginal Peoples’ connection to Land and Country, students develop respect for the practices and beliefs of others in their community.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. When teaching the nature and effect of interactions with the British regarding Aboriginal Peoples, the outcome requires students to identify Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation. Students engage with sources to identify some of the effects of colonisation on Aboriginal Peoples and group these according to access to Country, conflict with settlers, and the health and daily life of Aboriginal Peoples.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Botany Bay
  • Site study: Myall Creek Massacre Memorial Site, NSW
  • Case study: Pemulwuy
  • Case study: Gweagal shield
  • Case study: Local or regional group and the impact of colonisation on Aboriginal Peoples, 1788 –c. 1901.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • continuity and change – aspects of Aboriginal Peoples’ daily lives prior to and after the arrival of the British
  • cause and effect – the effect of colonisation on Traditional Aboriginal Languages
  • significance – Bennelong’s role in establishing relationships with British people.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation

  • The nature of interactions with the British regarding Aboriginal Peoples

Historical skills: Communication

  • use appropriate terminology when communicating information about Aboriginal Peoples
Teacher defines key terminology before identifying the terms in source information about Aboriginal Peoples interactions with the British. Students select appropriate terminology when identifying the nature of interactions between the British and Aboriginal Peoples.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills.

For example:

  • What role does Country play in Aboriginal Peoples’ spiritual and Cultural connections?
  • What impact did the initial interactions with the British have on Aboriginal Peoples’ health, wellbeing and spirituality?
  • What were the causes of the Frontier Wars?
  • How did colonisation impact the daily lives and Cultures of Aboriginal Peoples, families and Communities?

Connecting with Stage 4 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 4 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 4: Background and origins of Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia

  • The causes and locations of the Frontier Wars across Australia
Teachers guide students to select maps and relevant sources on the Frontier Wars. Students studying Stage 4 content create a multimodal presentation to locate and explain the causes and effects of colonisation that led to the Frontier Wars.

Life Skills: Background, origins and connections to Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia

  • Reasons for the Frontier Wars
Teachers select a written or multimodal source related to the Frontier Wars. Students studying Life Skills content use the source to create a list or mind map of reasons why Aboriginal People resisted the British arrival and occupation around Australia.

Purpose

In this focus area, students have the opportunity to build understanding of different perspectives as they engage with stories related to the time of Federation and Australia at war. They consider the experiences of others when investigating the impacts of World War I and Federation on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other groups. When sequencing events leading to Federation, students develop numeracy skills.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when exploring the ongoing legacy of ONE significant person, the outcome requires students to investigate the impact or legacy of a significant individual from the past. Students select an individual and engage with sources to identify their contributions to Australia. Students identify their impacts (represented on flashcards, images or manipulatives) and draw conclusions about their legacy.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to Australia can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to this focus area.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: A local historical site
  • Site study: A site of a significant battle in WWI
  • Case study: Impact of Federation on specific groups
  • Case study: Laws in Australia

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • continuity and change – similarities and differences in daily life in 19th century Australia and the present day
  • perspective – differing perspectives on Federation
  • significance – WWI battles in which Australians fought.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Australia: Making a nation

  • The impact of Federation or WWI on different groups in Australia, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

Historical skills: Perspectives and interpretations

  • recognise different perspectives within historical sources
Students engage with a range of propaganda material and sources related to Federation and identify if the source is for or against Federation. Using prompts and sentence starters, students identify the impact that Federation may have had on particular people according to the propaganda.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What does it mean to belong to a group?
  • Why were different groups in society for or against Federation?
  • How did WWI impact on daily life on the home front?
  • What were the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples in Australia?

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priority

Teachers and schools should work in partnership with local Aboriginal Communities when planning and teaching Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures. Refer to NESA’s Working with Aboriginal Communities for additional advice on working with Aboriginal Communities.

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • Nature, commemoration and perspectives of the Anzac legend
Students studying Stage 5 content engage with sources to develop their understanding of the origins of the Anzac legend, and how the concepts of mateship and sacrifice are commemorated. They explain how the Anzac legend has shaped national identity and consider military, cultural and historical perspectives.

Life Skills:

  • How memorials, remembrances and institutions in Australia today reflect WWI
Students studying Life Skills content explore a range of local and national Anzac memorials and remembrance ceremonies. They investigate why these memorials or ceremonies were established and how they honour the people or events of WWI.

Purpose

The medieval world (c. 500 – c. 1600) provides opportunities for students to develop skills in numeracy (time, sequencing, location and navigation) and literacy (reading and interpreting sources and creating texts). Exploring the roles of individuals and groups in medieval societies can assist the development of understanding and openness around the perspectives and ideas of others.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when teaching aspects of the daily life of Aztecs during the Spanish Conquest, the outcome requires students to investigate ways people lived. Students use sources to find out about a particular group of people (e.g. farmers, fisherman or craftsmen) and draw conclusions about their daily lives.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to the medieval world content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the selected society and key ideas.

Planning for teaching and learning

Information to guide planning for teaching and learning can be found in The medieval world (c. 500 – c. 1600) – Planning for teaching and learning.

Connecting with Stage 4 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 4 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 4

  • Create written texts to explain historical concepts related to the Black Death
  • The causes and symptoms of the Black Death
  • Daily life of men, women and children and life expectancy in the 14th century
Students studying Stage 4 content locate a range of sources and create a written text explaining cause and effect related to the Black Death. This may include identifying how the understanding of causes and symptoms, along with treatments and preventative measures, impacted on daily life and life expectancy of men, women and children. The written text may be in the form of a paragraph or a more extended text.

Life Skills

  • Communicate ideas about the medieval world through oral, visual, written or multimodal texts
  • Aspects of the daily life of men, women or children in the society or event
Students studying Life Skills content are provided with sources about the daily practices used by people to protect themselves from the Black Death. Students create a poster or slide deck, or select images, to communicate their findings.

Purpose

Students have opportunities to develop skills in numeracy by plotting significant dates of WWII on a timeline. Understanding of different perspectives can be developed when considering personal stories and experiences related to Australia at war.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when teaching about the uniforms, weaponry and transport used by Australian troops in WWII, the outcome requires students to identify the key features. Students may engage with a range of stimulus including objects, images, video or audio and respond to prompts and questions to name or select details of uniforms, weaponry and transport.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to Australia at war content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to Australia at war – WWII (1939 – c. 1945).

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: The Australian War Memorial Museum, Canberra
  • Site study: The Kokoda Track, Papua New Guinea
  • Case study: Experiences of Gunditjmarra man Captain Reg Saunders
  • Case study: Experiences of Quandamooka woman Oodegeroo Noonuccal
  • Case study: The Australian Women’s Army Service (AWAS)

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • cause and effect – reasons Australia went to war
  • perspective – differing experiences of Australian soldiers in WWII
  • significance – Yolngu soldiers united Aboriginal groups to defend Australia during WWII as the Northern Territory Special Reconnaissance Unit.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activity

Australia at war – WWII (1939 – c. 1945): Background, origins and connections to Australia at war

  • Personal or local stories related to Australia at war

Historical skills: Communication

  • communicate using language appropriate to purpose and audience
Students visit a local war memorial and gather the dates, locations and names of those who served. They identify and acknowledge the involvement of Aboriginal soldiers. Students communicate the different experiences of people during war to their peers to inform them, using appropriate language. They may be supported with sentence starters and visual and verbal prompts.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What was Australia’s response to the war?
  • How did life change for women and children when Australia was at war?
  • Why are specific sites or battles identified as significant for Australians?
  • How do we honour the sacrifice of soldiers from the wars?

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priority

Teachers and schools should work in partnership with local Aboriginal Communities when planning and teaching Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures. Refer to NESA’s Working with Aboriginal Communities for additional advice on working with Aboriginal Communities.

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • Reasons for the enlistment, and the experiences of servicemen and servicewomen in Australia’s defence forces, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
Students studying Stage 5 content learn about the enlistment, training, deployment, combat, support roles or home front roles of servicepeople including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples during WWII. They create a graphic organiser reporting on the various experiences and perspectives.

Life Skills:

  • Contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, women and migrants to WWII
Students studying Life Skills content learn about the different contributions made by groups on the home front and at war and represent their understanding using a graphic organiser.

Purpose

This focus area provides opportunities for students to develop numeracy and mapping skills when locating different countries and tracing journeys. They can explore self-advocacy when investigating various historical conflicts between nations. Understanding different perspectives can be explored when considering power and authority.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when exploring representations of Asian cultures and traditions in Australia, the outcome requires students to investigate the impact or legacy of a significant idea, event, individual or group from the past. Students engage with representations of Asian cultures such as food, festivals and celebrations held in Australia to draw conclusions about the legacy of Asian migrants who moved to Australia during this period.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to imperialism in Asia content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to Imperialism in Asia.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Tiananmen Square and the Forbidden City, Beijing
  • Case study: The influence of an Asian society on modern Australian culture
  • Case study: European exploration and colonisation of India
  • Case study: Trade between Europe and Asia

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – how the relationships between Asian countries have changed over time
  • cause and effect – how life in an Asian nation changed as a result of interactions with a European power
  • significance – the impact of an individual or group on an Asian society.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Imperialism in Asia (1750–1918):  Background, origins and connections to imperialism in Asia

  • The geographical location of significant nations in Asia

Historical skills: Communication

  • communicate ideas about people, events or societies
Students engage with a range of interactive maps and create a multimodal display identifying the names and locations of significant nations in Asia.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What are the individual connections students have with a particular Asian nation (family, friends, holidays, cultural connections or consumerism)?
  • What impact did encounters with a European nation have on daily life in an Asian nation?
  • Why did the British focus on India as a key colony?
  • Who were the Boxers in the Boxer Rebellion in China?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentTeaching and learning activity

Stage 5:

  • The role of European trading companies including the British East India Company and the Dutch East India Company in Asia in this period
Students studying Stage 5 content engage with a range of sources and create an infographic about the role of the British East India company. They explain why Britain wanted to trade with and in India, considering the purpose, advantages and risks for Britain.

Life Skills:

  • Resources produced by Asia that were used by other nations
Students studying Life Skills content engage with sources to identify resources found in India that were wanted in and used by Britain.
