Purpose

Teachers can develop a school-developed option that considers the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students. This provides opportunities for students to engage with historical people, places and events of personal interest and relevance.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are: Focus of study, Consider site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills, Consider historical inquiry processes, and Select the content.

Focus of study

Select an option, choose outcomes and define the focus.

For example:

  • Ancient Australia – Songlines and stories
  • Women in ancient and medieval times – Rulers, queens, warriors and maids
  • Experiences of migrants in Australia – Stories from local communities
  • Australia and the Vietnam War – commemoration and remembrance
  • Sport and the Australian Story – Sporting legends
  • Rights of people with disability – The history of the Paralympics
  • Technological change and development in 20th and 21st centuries – Telephones, transport and technology.

Consider a site study or case study

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Adventurers of Antarctica
  • Case study: Symbols and styles – Fashion from ancient and medieval times
  • Case study: Tilly Aston’s fight for rights for people who are blind in Australia

Consider historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

Select historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

Consider historical inquiry process

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills.

For example:

  • What were the primary causes of this event or development?
  • Why is the individual or event considered significant in history?
  • In what ways did the social, political or economic structures change over time?
  • How did different groups perceive this specific event or development?

Select content

Select content from the syllabus as appropriate to the outcomes, focus of study, site or case study, student learning needs and school context, considering:

  • backgrounds and origins
  • significant groups, individuals, ideas, beliefs, practices or events
  • impact and legacies.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Considerations may include:

  • scaffolds and supports for conducting research and participating in a collaborative inquiry
  • participating in part or whole of a historical inquiry
  • students communicating their learning using their preferred communication form(s)
  • encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when discussing ideas and planning for writing.

Connecting with Stage 4 and Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content integrated with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

For example, when engaging with a school-developed option about women in ancient and medieval times, students studying Life Skills content could locate sources to answer questions about the past, while students studying Stage 5 content could identify, locate, select and organise information from a variety of sources, including digital technologies and other methods.

This focus area provides opportunities for students to explore life in societies that were established in ancient times. Exploring the roles of individuals and groups can assist the development of understanding different perspectives and being open to the ideas of others.

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching about a society’s geographical features, the outcome requires students to identify its key features. When students engage with sources about the Nile River, they name the different ways the river was used by individuals and groups.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to the ancient society content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the selected society and key ideas.

Purpose

Students explore sustainability and ways to care for the environment to build community engagement and responsible citizenship. They develop decision-making and problem-solving skills as they explore environmental impacts on sites.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when students are exploring local activities or events that care for the environment, the outcome requires students to identify ways to engage with local and national issues. Students may focus on waste and recognise and name ways they can participate in local activities to reduce waste.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to The environmental movement content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the environmental movement.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: A local area impacted by environmental change
  • Site study: Machu Picchu, Peru
  • Case study: Aboriginal ways of caring for Country
  • Case study: Earth Day

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

  • continuity and change – changes in environmental movements from 1960 to today
  • cause and effect – the impact of protests on popular views of environmental issues
  • perspective – the need for environmental protection of specific regions or species
  • significance – the impact of an individual or group on public views about the environment.

Historical skills

Historical skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

The environmental movement (c. 1960 – c. 2015): Background, origins and connections to the environmental movement

  • A site that has been impacted by environmental change

Historical skills: Communication

  • communicate ideas about people, events or societies
Students explore images of a site that has been impacted by environmental change. Sites could include Port Arthur, Rapa Nui and Venice. They communicate ideas about environmental change by gesturing to, pointing to or naming key features that have changed.

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • Why should the environment be protected?
  • How have issues have been addressed by the environmental movement?
  • Which groups have protected the environment in Australia and what have they achieved?
  • What is Australia’s role in environmental protection in Australia and globally?

Purpose

By exploring the persecution of Jewish people by Nazi Germany during the Holocaust, students have the opportunity to build their understanding of justice, equity, resilience and advocacy. They can develop skills to regulate emotional responses and effectively communicate in situations in which they or others are not being treated equitably or fairly.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when exploring survivor stories of people affected by the Holocaust, the outcome requires students to investigate the impact or legacy of a significant idea, event, individual or group from the past. The teacher shares examples of bravery, hope and resilience from the Holocaust. Students explore sources and develop an understanding of the impact of the Holocaust on survivors.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to the Holocaust content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the Holocaust.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Online Jewish museums
  • Site study: Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Poland
  • Case study: Anne Frank
  • Case study: Oskar Schindler
  • Case study: Yorta Yorta elder William Cooper’s protest against Nazi treatment of Jewish people

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example: 

  • continuity and change – life in Germany for Jewish People before, during and immediately following the Holocaust
  • cause and effect – the impact of Nazi policies on daily life for all members of the community
  • perspective – stories of Holocaust survivors
  • significance – remembrance, legacy and life lessons from the Holocaust.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activity

The Holocaust (1933–1945): Significant groups, individuals, ideas, beliefs, practices or events in the Holocaust

  • Jewish resistance during the Holocaust
  • The contributions of a significant individual or group

Historical skills: Comprehension – chronology, terms and concepts

  • engage with historical texts
Students engage with stories and accounts from people who experienced the Holocaust, including members of the Jewish resistance and those who made significant contributions by helping others in need. Students respond to who, what, when, where, why and how prompts to identify details about the Jewish resistance and others who helped during the Holocaust.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • Why are human rights important and how can they be protected and upheld?
  • How can students take action in their own lives and communities to demonstrate upstander behaviour?
  • What role did bystanders and upstanders play during the Holocaust?
  • How do we remember and honour the victims and survivors of the Holocaust?

They investigate the impact of the Holocaust on the Jewish people by exploring an exhibition that commemorates the Holocaust. They identify associated organisations and events that commemorate the Holocaust and ways they could be involved.

Purpose

Students have opportunities to develop numeracy skills by sequencing the development of inventions. Students may apply literacy skills to create texts about inventions of their choice, incorporating specific vocabulary. Understanding of different perspectives can be developed when engaging with sources showing the various experiences of individuals and groups during the Industrial Revolution.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when exploring a specific technological invention that occurred during the Industrial Revolution and how it changed society, the outcome requires students to recognise continuity and change. Students view images of a task being done before and after the introduction of a specific technological invention such as the telephone and point to, circle or name what has changed and what has stayed the same.

Making connections

Content from the Background, origins and connections to the Industrial Revolution content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the event and key ideas.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: The Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace, London
  • Case study: The working life of children during the Industrial Revolution
  • Case study: The development of an invention such as the steam engine
  • Case study: A profile of an inventor such as Thomas Edison

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – how a task changed after the introduction of a new technology and which tasks stayed the same
  • cause and effect – the impact of production of goods in factories
  • perspective – differing views of groups of people on a technological advancement
  • significance – assembly line production and its influence on manufacturing.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

The Industrial Revolution (1750–1850): Significant groups, individuals, ideas, beliefs, practices or events in the Industrial Revolution

  • Groups of people who were affected by the Industrial Revolution

Historical skills: Research

  • recognise sources of information about past events
  • use sources to answer questions about the past
Students are presented with a range of sources about working conditions for children in factories. They identify information provided by these sources and answer questions about working conditions for children during the Industrial Revolution.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • What were the most important inventions and technologies that were developed during the Industrial Revolution and why?
  • How do we use technology in daily life?
  • Why did daily life change during the Industrial Revolution?
  • Who did the most dangerous jobs in Britain during the Industrial Revolution?

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

  • The British Agricultural Revolution, population movements and changing patterns of settlement in Britain

They create a flow chart identifying the components of and inter-relationship between the changes in population movement and settlement patterns that occurred due to the Agricultural Revolution.

  • How the daily lives of workers, including women and children, changed during the Industrial Revolution
Students studying Life Skills content engage with a range of sources showing how daily life changed during the Industrial Revolution in an agricultural context. The teacher may use questioning and prompting to support students to identify how life changed for inventors, farm workers, traders, craftsmen, children, women, upper class people or working class people.

content.value:
Purpose

Students have opportunities to develop communication skills when engaging with others and sharing opinions and ideas about the movement of peoples. Understanding of different perspectives can be developed when considering the groups and individuals affected by the movement of peoples.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when considering the impacts of convict or slave labour, the outcome requires students to identify different contexts and perspectives of the past. The teacher shares reasons why individuals and groups either supported or opposed convict and slave labour. Students engage in matching and sorting activities to identify different perspectives.

Making connections

Content from the Backgrounds, origins and connections to the movement of peoples content group can be used to build students’ understanding and connections to the Movement of peoples.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Port Arthur, Tasmania
  • Site study: Hyde Park Barracks, Sydney
  • Case study: Investigate the story of a slave, convict or free settler
  • Case study: Stories of people who have come to Australia

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – similarities and differences in journeys to Australia in the 19th century and the present day
  • cause and effect – reasons for people moving from one place to another including unforced and forced movement
  • perspective – differing perspectives of free settlers and convicts on coming to Australia
  • significance – the establishment of the first penal colony at Sydney Cove.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities. 

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

The movement of peoples (1750–1901): Background, origins and connections to the movement of peoples

  • The geographical location and countries involved in the movement of peoples

Historical skills: Comprehension – chronology, terms and concepts

  • use appropriate historical terms and concepts to communicate about the past
Students work collaboratively to identify where people came from and where they moved to during a particular time period. Key terms such as slaves, convicts and free settlers are defined, and understanding is supported using a range of visual, written and digital activities and resources. Students create statements about the movement of peoples, using key terms.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills.

For example:

  • How did countries and colonies benefit from forced and unforced migration?
  • What were the effects of slave labour on the individual and families?
  • Who was against slave labour and why?
  • Why do people move in modern times?

Connecting with Stage 5 History

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 4 or 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 4 or 5 History outcomes.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5:

  • Differing experiences of enslaved people, convicts, emancipists and free settlers
Students studying Stage 5 content engage with a range of sources to identify individual experiences of departure, journey and treatment on arrival. Students give reasons why the experiences and perspectives differed between individuals and groups.

Life Skills:

  • Aspects of the daily living or working conditions of free settlers, convicts or enslaved people, including women
Students studying Life Skills content engage with sources related to living conditions of free settlers, convicts or enslaved people. They create a storyboard depicting an aspect of daily living of free settlers, convicts or enslaved people, including women. Visual supports may assist students to sequence the storyboard.

Purpose

This focus area provides opportunities for students to develop their self-awareness by engaging with stories, objects, images, written documents or digital recordings related to their local history. Recognising similarities and differences between their own lives and life in the past supports students to understand different perspectives. Communicating about their local history can consolidate their connections to others.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Focus of study

The outcomes determine the scope of learning for the content points. For example, when exploring the chronology of significant events in the recent past, the outcome requires students to sequence events in chronological order. Students use visuals and manipulatives (representing activities and events) to arrange into first/then order or place on a timeline.

Planning for teaching and learning

The following process may be helpful when planning teaching and learning for this focus area.

Image long description: The steps in planning for teaching and learning appear in boxes. Arrows pointing from left to right appear in between each box. The steps are Choose site or case studies, Consider historical concepts, Select historical skills and Consider historical inquiry processes.

Site and case studies

A site study or case study can be used to support understanding of the key ideas.

For example:

  • Site study: Local Aboriginal site of significance – teachers and schools should work in partnership with local Aboriginal Communities when planning and teaching Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures
  • Site study: Local community site or historical event
  • Site study: Site or event of family significance
  • Case study: Interview with an older family or community member about their life experiences
  • Case study: Impact of a key person or event in history on life today, such as:
    • Sir Isaac Newton
    • Rosalind Franklin
    • the development of vaccines
    • the evolution of communication technology from telegrams to texts
    • the printing press

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. 

For example:

  • continuity and change – what has changed and what has stayed the same at a local site over time
  • cause and effect – factors that caused a local site to change over time
  • significance – people and events in own personal history.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

The past in the present: Working with historical concepts and skills

  • Communicate ideas about the past through oral, visual, written or multimodal texts

Historical skills: Comprehension – chronology, terms and concepts

  • use units of time to describe the recent past
  • sequence past events in chronological order

Historical skills: Analysis and use of sources

  • locate information in a source

Students access sources of local history, such as videos, photographs, objects or artefacts, to identify significant events in their local history.

They create a timeline of these events using images, audio or video recordings and/or written text.

Historical inquiry

Opportunities to engage in an aspect of historical inquiry can be included. Develop inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills. 

For example:

  • Why is it important to know about personal, family or local history?
  • How has daily life for individuals and families changed from the past to today?
  • What has changed and what has stayed the same in the local area from the past to today?
  • How do we use sources to find information about the past?

Connecting with Stage 4 and Stage 5 History

This focus area is unique to History 7–10 Life Skills. If required, the content can be taught with the Stage 4 or Stage 5 content when developing students’ understanding of historical sources and historical inquiry to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. For example, students studying Life Skills content could identify information in a source while students studying Stage 5 content process information from a range of sources as evidence in a historical argument.

Content focus

The core depth study Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia focuses on enhancing students’ historical knowledge and skills through an immersive study of Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia. This knowledge builds on content studied in Sources of evidence on how people lived in the first penal settlement at Sydney Cove (HSIE Stage 2) and can be enriched through a choice of a case study or site study.

The following knowledge and understanding content supports learning in the focus area:

  • Historical context 3 (core): The era of colonisation.

Key ideas

  • Different ways Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people view Country
  • The influence of the concept of terra nullius on British colonisation policies
  • Aboriginal resistance, resilience and strategic responses to the Frontier Wars
  • Significant conflicts such as Sydney Cove, Tasmania and Myall Creek
  • Immediate and long-term effects of the establishment of missions, stations, reserves and the Aborigines Protection Board (APB)

Key terms

  • Aborigines Protection Board (APB)
  • Black War
  • colonisation
  • Country
  • Culture
  • dispossession
  • invasion
  • Kinship
  • missions, reserves and stations
  • resistance
  • sovereignty
  • Terra Nullius
  • Traditional Custodians

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – continuity and survival of Cultural Practices and Languages
  • Cause and effect – the nature and course of the Frontier Wars
  • Perspectives – experiences of key Aboriginal Peoples through the examination of sources
  • Significance – the Myall Creek Massacre and its impact on the NSW and Australian legal system
  • Contestability – doctrine of terra nullius and the nature of Aboriginal Peoples’ resistance.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline that sequences key events from the arrival of the First Fleet to the establishment of the Aborigines Protection Board in NSW
  • exploring the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) map of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Language groups and locating where the Black War and Frontier Wars were fought
  • researching the agency and impact of a key identity involved in Aboriginal resistance
  • selecting examples of sources, such as colonial government records, mission records, newspapers, letters, diaries and testimonies to compare and contrast treatment and rights of Aboriginal People living on missions, reserves and stations such as the Cummeragunja Mission in NSW
  • evaluating the reliability and limitations of a missionary’s diary as a source for understanding Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences in this period
  • discussing how historical interpretations of the Myall Creek Massacre have changed over time
  • discussing the ethical considerations involved in using Oral Histories from Aboriginal Elders in research.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • What is the meaning of Connection to Country for Aboriginal Peoples?
  • How have Aboriginal Peoples resisted British colonisation?
  • What were the consequences of British expansion into Tasmania including dispossession, disease and removal to the Bass Strait?
  • What are the perspectives on the role of religious organisations during this period of colonisation, according to historical sources?
  • How did the policies of the Aborigines Protection Board in NSW impact Aboriginal Peoples?
  • How did missions, reserves and stations alter Aboriginal Peoples’ lives and society?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Aboriginal cricket team’s ‘Tour of England’ of 1868
  • The impact of colonisation on Aboriginal Languages and the use of Aboriginal English  
  • The impact of missionary schools on Aboriginal children
  • The removal and repatriation of items such as the Gweagal shield and the Kamay spears from Custodians
  • Appin (Dharawal) Massacre Memorial Monument, Cataract Dam, NSW
  • La Perouse Museum and Bare Island, Sydney
  • Museums of History NSW (MHNSW), Sydney
  • Myall Creek Massacre and Memorial Site, Bingara, NSW

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures content supports students in developing knowledge about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Cultures and highlights the significance and connections to local Aboriginal Community contexts, creating meaningful learning opportunities.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by providing opportunities for them to interrogate evidence from sources to draw conclusions about groups, individuals or events relevant to the Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation.

Historical concepts are integral to the development of historical understanding. Knowledge and understanding, concepts and skills are interrelated and should be taught in an integrated way to provide meaningful learning experiences for students.

The concepts are ideas or themes that can be applied across the syllabus to identify questions, guide investigations and interpret findings. The concepts arise naturally from the content and are not meant to be taught as content in isolation.

Students use historical concepts to describe and explain the past for a range of purposes, audiences and contexts. Students may be extended through comparative analysis, evaluations and creative pursuits.

Teachers are encouraged to identify relevant concepts related to the content of each focus area. The selected historical concepts should align with the content and enable students to view and analyse the world through a particular lens. Teachers should encourage students to consider why the learning matters. This supports the development of historical thinking.

Content focus

The purpose of this historical context study is to develop historical knowledge related to the ancient past. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of one or 2 depth studies, a case study or site study.

The ancient past core context study focuses on exploring ancient societies through historical inquiry, encompassing the use of sources and understanding of historical concepts and skills. Depth study options include ancient Egypt, ancient India, ancient China, ancient Greece and ancient Rome.

Building knowledge

This context study builds on the content covered in People use stories, images and sites to understand the ancient past (HSIE Stage 1). The ancient world laid the foundations of culture, governance, and social structures, influencing later societies globally.

Key ideas

  • Migration and the global development of settlements and societies
  • Methods used by historians and archaeologists to study the past
  • Impact of technological advancement on archaeological practices
  • Removal and repatriation of cultural artefacts and human remains
  • Changing role of museums in collecting, preserving and displaying objects of significance

Key terms

  • archaeology
  • artefacts
  • chronology
  • conservation
  • historical inquiry
  • iconography
  • Oral tradition
  • periodisation
  • preservation
  • repatriation

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – examination of archaeological sites and objects that show evidence that Aboriginal Peoples are the oldest living, continuous Cultures in the world
  • Cause and effect – impact of changing archaeological practices and use of modern technologies to understand the past
  • Perspectives – preservation and exhibition of objects of cultural importance
  • Significance – early historians’ methods of historical inquiry
  • Contestability – ownership of artefacts and return of objects of historical importance to original owners.

Historical skills

Suggested application of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline showing major historical periods that categorise ancient times
  • discussing different modern technologies and the role that experts such as archaeologists, anthropologists, cryptographers, historians, scientists and museum curators have in recording history
  • identifying and describing different perspectives and arguments for conserving the past
  • researching a specific topic related to the ancient world, such as farming or hunter-gatherer societies, ancient economies, the agency and status of women and children, or ancient innovations
  • curating an audio, visual or written guide for a specific ancient artefact in a museum exhibit, communicating its historical importance, cultural context and impact on the ancient world.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • How do archaeological discoveries provide evidence for theories of human migration and the development of societies worldwide?
  • How can historical sources such as art, iconography, oral tradition and archaeological artefacts be used to gain insight into the past?
  • How do concepts of chronology and periodisation help to organise and interpret historical events and developments?
  • What are the key features of Aboriginal Cultures, Knowledges and Histories, and how do they contribute to our understanding of ancient societies?
  • What are the reasons behind the removal of cultural artefacts, and what are the social, cultural and ethical implications of this practice?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Oral traditions
  • Civic engagement across the ancient world
  • Herodotus as the ‘father of history’
  • Mungo Lady and Mungo Man
  • The Code of Hammurabi (Mesopotamia)
  • Brewarrina Fish Traps (Baiame’s Ngunnhu), Australia
  • Australian Museum, Sydney
  • Machu Picchu, Peru
  • National Museum of Australia, Canberra
  • Rapa Nui (Easter Island), Chile
  • Willandra Lakes Region, NSW 

Considerations for teaching and learning 

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures content supports students in developing knowledge about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Cultures and highlights the significance and connections to local Aboriginal Community contexts, creating meaningful learning opportunities.
  • Providing opportunities for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to the focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students through activities related to comparative analysis of different methods for preserving and conserving archaeological and historical remains.

Content focus

The purpose of this Historical context study is to develop historical knowledge related to the medieval world. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a depth study, case study or site study related to a medieval society.

The medieval world core context study focuses on exploring medieval times through historical inquiry, encompassing the use of sources and understanding of historical concepts and skills. Depth study options include Medieval Europe, The expansion of Islam, Polynesian expansion across the Pacific, The Vikings, The Angkor/Khmer Empire, Japan under the Shoguns, Mongol expansion, The Ottoman Empire, The Black Death in Asia, Europe and North Africa, Renaissance Italy and The Spanish conquest of the Americas.

Building knowledge

This context study builds on the content covered in Historical context study 1 (core): The ancient past and depth study options. The medieval world is characterised by feudalism, the spread of Christianity, power and authority of the monarch and the Church and the expansion of Islam.

Key ideas

  • Social structures and religious dominance under feudalism
  • Reasons for the growth of towns and cities
  • Cross-cultural interactions, networks and impacts of trade and communication across the world
  • Transformation of European society including the impact of the Reformation

Key terms

  • caliphate
  • Christendom
  • Crusades
  • feudalism
  • heresy
  • Magna Carta
  • monarchy
  • monastery
  • Reformation
  • Renaissance
  • Silk Roads
  • social hierarchy
  • trade route

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – social hierarchies and the role and status of men, women and children across the globe during this period
  • Cause and effect – collapse of the Roman Empire leading to a power vacuum and development of feudalism
  • Perspectives – experiences of cross-cultural contact through trade routes
  • Significance – expansion of Islam in the Middle East, North Africa and Spain and the spread of Arabic language, knowledge and trade
  • Contestability – Christianity as either a unifying or dividing force in post-Roman European society.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline showing the major changes that categorise the medieval era
  • using interactive maps to trace the routes of medieval trade networks and identify the goods and ideas exchanged between Europe, Asia and Africa
  • reading historical texts on the sources of social hierarchies during medieval times and drawing conclusions on the status and agency of women 
  • selecting examples of artefacts such as illuminated manuscripts, armour, medieval weaponry and architectural remnants and explaining their function and significance in medieval society
  • comparing and contrasting European and Asian feudal systems through researching similarities and differences in peoples’ daily lives
  • creating a diagram presenting reasons for and against King John I’s signing of the Magna Carta
  • researching the impact of technological innovations such as the printing press, the compass and the waterwheel on medieval society.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • How was Christianity dominant in the lives of people living in Europe during medieval times?
  • What led to the expansion of Islam in medieval times?
  • How did social hierarchies form and transform the lives of people living in medieval times?
  • How did different societies interact during medieval times?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Heresy and witchcraft in Germany, France, Switzerland, England and/or Scotland
  • The Children’s Crusade
  • The sack of Constantinople
  • The travels of Marco Polo
  • Alhambra, Granada, Spain
  • Canterbury Cathedral, England
  • Krak des Chevaliers, Syria
  • Notre Dame, Paris, France 
  • Warwick Castle, England

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to the focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by discussing or debating perspectives of individuals they have researched using sources relevant to the medieval world.

Content focus

The purpose of this Historical context study is to develop historical knowledge related to the era of colonisation. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a case study or site study.

The focus of this context study is the nature and impact of European exploration and International Indigenous Peoples’ response to colonisation. The core depth study of Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia supports deeper learning about this time.

Building knowledge

This context study builds on the content covered in Historical sources present perspectives on the past (HSIE Stage 3), Historical context study 2 (core) The medieval world. The era of colonisation saw European powers expand their territories globally as a result of monarchs’ ambitions and papal decrees. The British colonisation of Australia began in 1788, impacting Aboriginal Peoples and shaping the nation’s development.

Key idea

  • Reasons driving European exploration
  • The nature and significance of resistance and warfare in colonised territories

Key terms

  • colonisation
  • Doctrine of Discovery
  • empire
  • exploitation
  • exploration
  • International Indigenous People
  • resistance

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – experiences of ONE International Indigenous community after conquest
  • Cause and effect – consequences of new trade routes on European exploration
  • Perspectives – views from relevant sources on ONE explorer
  • Significance – arrival of European missionaries in the Pacific region
  • Contestability – historical interpretations of reasons for European expansion.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline showing the major events that categorise the ‘era of colonisation’
  • selecting sources such as letters, diaries or treaties related to the colonisation of South-East Asia to identify origin, context and purpose of each source
  • researching the impact of colonisation on the trade routes in the Indian and Pacific Oceans
  • creating a multimedia presentation on the colonisation of one International Indigenous community incorporating oral, graphic, written and digital elements to effectively communicate findings.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • In what ways did European colonisation change political, economic and social structures?
  • What were the primary motivations behind European exploration and how did technological, political and cultural factors contribute to their colonial ambitions?
  • How did the Doctrine of Discovery legitimise European claims to non-European lands?
  • How did International Indigenous communities adapt to and resist European colonisation?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Establishment of plantation economies and the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade
  • The New Zealand Wars and the Treaty of Waitangi
  • The Scramble for Africa and the Berlin Conference
  • The spice trade in the East Indies
  • British Museum, England
  • Elmina Castle, Ghana
  • Museums of History NSW (MHNSW), Sydney
  • Williamsburg, Virginia, USA

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures content supports students to develop knowledge about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Cultures and highlights the significance and connections to local Aboriginal Community contexts, creating meaningful learning opportunities.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to the focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and to use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by debating ethical and legal implications of colonisation.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Through historical inquiry, students make connections, construct coherent accounts and explanations of the past and deepen their knowledge and understanding of history. The stages of historical inquiry include:

Historical inquiry is an active process which enables students to question, interpret, describe, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. This process is to be integrated with syllabus content and explicitly taught. The focus areas provide a context for developing and applying these inquiry skills.

It is suggested that teachers:

  • explicitly teach students to think historically by developing the critical skills of inquiry into the past.
  • consider the accessibility of sources for historical inquiry, including readability levels of written materials, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions for videos, and tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources.
  • guide students to explain the meaning and context of sources as part of a historical inquiry.
  • present students with a range of appropriate sources and assist students in applying ethical consideration and practices in their own research.
  • demonstrate how to interpret sources, drawing students’ attention to the value and limitations of selected sources.
  • explicitly teach students how to construct valid interpretations and perspectives using sound evidence gathered from primary and secondary sources.
  • encourage students to present their findings and ideas, drawing conclusions and citing evidence from credible sources.
  • encourage students to develop their creative and critical thinking skills in order to present findings.
  • provide scaffolds and prompts to assist students to reflect and evaluate findings, and to communicate findings using relevant historical terms and concepts.

Guided discussion and debates are useful strategies to support students to consider contestability. This assists students in drawing conclusions about historical evidence as they learn to understand multiple perspectives, assess the credibility of these perspectives and provide informed accounts of the past based on evidence.

Important questions for teachers to pose when teaching students about historical inquiry could include:

  • What specific historical event, individual, period or topic will be the focus of the inquiry?
  • What do you know about the topic and what more do you hope to learn?
  • Which historical concepts will you apply to your inquiry?
  • How will you use selected sources?
  • What is the intended audience for each source selected and how does this influence your interpretation?
  • What themes will you use to organise your information?
  • How will you present your findings?
  • What historical terms, concepts and information from the sources located will you include in your findings?
  • How has your understanding of the chosen topic deepened as a result of your research?
  • What challenges did you encounter and how did you overcome them?

Suggested applications of historical inquiry questions are outlined in the teaching advice for each focus area.

Content focus

The core depth study Australia at war – WWII focuses on enhancing students’ historical knowledge and skills through an immersive study of Australia in WWII. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a case study or site study.

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area:

Historical context 4 (core): The making of the modern world

  • The rise of nation-states
  • The causes of the First World War
  • The impact of the Paris Peace Conference in shaping the world after WWI
  • Reasons for the proliferation of political ideologies in the interwar period

Key ideas

  • The causes of WWII and the reasons for Australia’s involvement
  • Australia’s contribution and involvement in the Allied forces against the Axis powers
  • War in the Pacific and the internal and external threats to Australian security
  • The experiences of different groups during WWII
  • The challenges faced on the Australian home front
  • Post-war effects on returning personnel and Holocaust survivors in Australia
  • The significance of the Nuremberg trials and the Genocide Convention

Key terms

  • antisemitism
  • appeasement
  • battalion
  • censorship
  • concentration camp
  • conscription
  • enemy alien
  • fascism
  • genocide
  • home front
  • infantry
  • internment camp
  • propaganda
  • rationing

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – the interwar period in Australia including the Great Depression and the rise of extreme political groups and ideologies
  • Cause and effect – impact of the fall of Singapore for Allied forces and for Australia
  • Perspectives – servicemen and servicewomen, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ experiences in Australia’s defence forces
  • Significance – introduction of war time conscription on national unity and the political landscape
  • Contestability – debate over the Battle for Australia 1942 and its commemoration since 2008.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • sequencing key events and developments of WWII using a timeline and identifying key places where Australians fought on a map
  • identifying the origin, content, context and purpose of sources related to WWII and evaluating the reliability, value and limitations of these sources 
  • identifying and analysing the reasons for different perspectives and interpretations of the Bombing of Darwin and submarine attacks in Sydney and Newcastle
  • researching the experiences of an individual or group during WWII
  • researching and comparing the strategies and policies of wartime Prime Ministers: Robert Menzies, Arthur Fadden, John Curtin and Ben Chifley
  • researching the Palm Island Aboriginal Settlement in Queensland and resettlement of Aboriginal Peoples following Japanese attacks
  • designing a museum exhibition related to an aspect of Australia’s involvement in WWII.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • What was the nature of Australia’s involvement in WWII?
  • What motivated people to enlist in Australia’s defence forces in WWII?
  • What was the significance of the Fall of Singapore to Australia?
  • What was the impact of WWII on the Australian home front?
  • What were the experiences of prisoners of war during WWII?
  • What lasting effects did the Holocaust and the Nuremberg trials have on Australia?
  • What did the treatment of returning soldiers, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander personnel highlight?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Raphael Lemkin and defining ‘genocide’
  • Internment of Japanese, German and Italian Australians
  • Women during WWII including in the military (WAAAF, AWAS, WRANS), the Women’s Land Army and factory work
  • The effects of the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, including human health and environmental impact  
  • Australian National Maritime Museum, Sydney
  • Australian War Memorial, Canberra
  • Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park, Japan
  • Kokoda Track Memorial Walkway, Sydney
  • Nackeroo Memorial Monument, Timber Creek, Northern Territory
  • Yad Vashem Remembrance Centre, Jerusalem

Considerations for teaching and learning 

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by engaging them in an analysis of historians’ changing interpretations of Australia's role in WWII.

Content focus

The core depth study Australia: making a nation – from Federation to WWI focuses on enhancing students’ historical knowledge and skills through an immersive study of the impact of Federation and WWI on Australian society. This knowledge builds on content studied in People in Australia have democratic roles and responsibilities (HSIE Stage 3) and can be enriched through the choice of a case study or site study.

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area:

Historical context 4 (core): The making of the modern world

  • The consequences of the Industrial Revolution on living and working conditions
  • The impact of imperialism, immigration and slavery on the movement of peoples
  • The American Revolutionary War and the French Revolution as a foundation for modern day human rights, rule of law in governance and democratic ideals
  • The rise of nation-states
  • The causes of the First World War

Key ideas

  • Development of democracy and factors leading to Federation in Australia
  • Impact of significant legislation and reform for different groups
  • Australia’s involvement in the First World War
  • Debates on conscription and the war effort on the home front during WWI
  • Contributions of different groups and individuals to civic responsibilities
  • Legacy of the Anzacs

Key terms

  • Anzac
  • conscription
  • constitution
  • democracy
  • division of powers
  • egalitarianism
  • Federation
  • plebiscite
  • referendum
  • separation of powers
  • trade unions

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – Australian democracy and the continuation of democratic principles
  • Cause and effect – Australia’s decision to federate
  • Perspectives – views of politicians, soldiers and civilians regarding Australia’s involvement in WWI
  • Significance – establishment of the Australian Red Cross and the legacy of humanitarian aid and civic engagement
  • Contestability – reasons for the government’s uses of plebiscites and referendums in this period.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline from Federation to the Treaty of Peace Act (Germany) confirming Australia as a sovereign nation in the League of Nations
  • analysing population and voting data to understand Australia’s decision to federate and the political landscape from 1889 to the end of WWI
  • locating newspaper articles from WWI about the conscription debate, identifying the origin, context and purpose of each source and the value and limitation of the sources in understanding public opinion
  • researching the role of the Harvester Case (Ex parte HV McKay) and trade unions in protection of workers’ rights, including non-citizens  
  • explaining the relationship between the Federation of Australia and its involvement in WWI
  • creating a digital exhibition, incorporating text, images and interactive elements, that showcases the rights, roles and contributions of women in this period.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • What were the primary motivations behind the push for Federation in Australia?
  • How did the features of the Australian Constitution shape the government and society?
  • In what ways did the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 and the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 reflect social and political values during this time?
  • How did the rights and roles of women, migrants and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples change during this time?
  • How was the decision to become involved in WWI received domestically?
  • How did the debates over conscription and the War Precautions Act 1914 demonstrate democratic process and political tensions in Australia during WWI?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • NSW Parliament – legislation and reform in this period
  • Relief movements as part of the humanitarian response to WWI
  • The Australian Flying Corps in WWI
  • The legacy of the Magna Carta in Australia
  • Australian Government response to 1918 pneumonic influenza epidemic
  • Anzac Cove, Türkiye
  • Australian War Memorial, Canberra
  • Federation Pavilion, Centennial Park, Sydney
  • Old Parliament House, Canberra
  • Local WWI memorial
  • National Museum of Australia, Canberra
  • NSW Parliament House, Sydney
  • Sir Henry Parkes Memorial School of Arts, Tenterfield


Considerations for teaching and learning 

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by providing opportunities to analyse the ethics of war time conscription.

Content focus

The core depth study Human rights and freedoms focuses on enhancing students’ historical knowledge and skills through an immersive study of human rights and freedoms. This knowledge builds on content studied in Aboriginal Peoples’ experiences of colonisation in Australia (History Stage 4). This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a case study or site study related to this focus area.

The following knowledge and understanding supports learning in this focus area:

Historical context 5 (core): The modern world

  • Rise of movements for civil, political, social, cultural and economic rights in Australia and globally

Key ideas

  • The effect of government policies of protectionism and assimilation on Aboriginal Peoples’ human rights and freedoms
  • Aboriginal protest and resistance since 1938, including Day of Mourning
  • Key features of the US Civil Rights Movement and its influence on Australia 
  • The denial of human rights experienced by Aboriginal Peoples, including the experiences of the Stolen Generations and the struggle for land rights
  • Actions taken by individuals and groups in the struggle for human rights and freedoms
  • Impact of inequality on the lives of Aboriginal Peoples, including the denial of access to Language and Cultural expression

Key terms

  • assimilation policy
  • intergenerational trauma
  • protectionist policy
  • reconciliation policy
  • self-determination
  • sovereignty

Working with historical concepts and skills

Working with historical concepts and skills content is provided in each focus area and outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – the enduring resistance and resilience of Aboriginal Peoples
  • Cause and effect – effects of the assimilation policy on the Stolen Generations and the ongoing impact of intergenerational trauma on Aboriginal Peoples
  • Perspectives – Aboriginal Peoples’ differing views on land rights and sovereignty
  • Significance – 1967 Referendum
  • Contestability – limitations of international human rights conventions

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline of key events for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples from the Day of Mourning to the Uluru Statement from the Heart
  • researching the role of key activists such as Sir William Cooper, Jack Patten, William Ferguson, Sir Douglas Nicholls, Margaret Tucker and Pearl Mary ‘Gambanyi’ Gibbs
  • locating sources such as speeches, media releases and photos from the 1963 March on Washington and the passage of the Civil Rights Act 1964 (USA) to consider the influence of the American Civil Rights movement in Australia
  • using sources such as photographs, posters and media to discuss the struggles faced by the 1965 Freedom Riders
  • analysing sources from members of the Stolen Generations detailing their experiences in various institutions including Bomaderry Aboriginal Children’s Home
  • listening and reading Stolen Generations survivor testimonies collected in the Bringing Them Home Report to draw conclusions about the experiences of the survivors
  • discussing the various reactions from Aboriginal Peoples, non-Aboriginal Australians, industry groups and political parties to the Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) decision
  • analysing the significance of the Redfern Speech (1992) as a turning point in reconciliation and acknowledgement of dispossession
  • researching the struggle for rights and freedoms of a group in Australia or globally.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • What were the demands of the Day of Mourning protest in 1938?
  • How did the 1965 Freedom Ride and the 1967 Referendum change the legal and political landscape for Aboriginal Peoples in Australia?
  • What were the immediate and long-term experiences of Aboriginal Peoples who were forcibly removed as part of the assimilation policy?
  • How did the Bringing Them Home Report contribute to a national understanding of the experiences of the Stolen Generations?
  • What was the significance of the 2008 National Apology to the Stolen Generations?
  • What are the key factors that shaped the struggle for human rights and freedoms of a group in Australia or globally?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Aboriginal Languages revitalisation
  • Ann Curthoys’ Freedom Ride diary
  • Australian Human Rights Commission public inquiry – Toomelah Report
  • The Gurindji Strike (Wave Hill Walk-Off)
  • United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007)
  • Aboriginal Tent Embassy, Canberra
  • Coota Girls Aboriginal Corporation, NSW
  • Kinchela Boys Home Aboriginal Corporation (KBHAC), NSW
  • Museums of History New South Wales (MHNSW), Sydney
  • National Museum of Australia, Canberra

Considerations for teaching and learning 

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures content supports students in developing knowledge about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Cultures and highlights the significance and connections to local Aboriginal Community contexts, creating meaningful learning opportunities.
  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and to use their home language when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by encouraging them to conduct a comparative analysis of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land rights movements in Australia and an International Indigenous group worldwide.

Content focus

The purpose of this historical context study is to develop historical knowledge related to the making of the modern world. This knowledge can be enriched through the choice of a depth study, case study or site study.

The focus of this context study is the transformation of the world through industrialisation, imperialism, revolutions and two world wars. The focus area includes 2 core depth studies, Australia: making a nation – from Federation to WWI, and Australia at war – WWII. Depth study options include The Industrial Revolution, The movement of peoples, Imperialism in Asia, Key ideas and movements, and The Holocaust.

Building knowledge

This context study builds on the content covered in historical context study 3 (core) The era of colonisation. The making of the modern world was marked by rapid technological change, rise of nation states and the fall of empires, social upheaval and global conflicts. In this period Australia evolved from a British colony to a federated nation.

Key ideas

  • Impact of the Industrial Revolution on technology, urbanisation, labour conditions and social structures
  • Formation of nation-states and their influence on global politics and economies
  • The role of militarism, alliances, nationalism and imperialism in the lead up to the First World War
  • The changing geopolitical landscape following WWI
  • The interwar period including the Great Depression

Key terms

  • alliances
  • colonialism
  • democracy
  • geopolitical
  • imperialism
  • League of Nations
  • militarism
  • modernisation
  • nationalism
  • revolution
  • slavery

Working with historical concepts and skills

Thinking and working historically is outlined in each focus area. It outlines how historical concepts, historical skills and historical inquiry can be integrated into the focus area.

Historical concepts

Suggested applications of historical concepts for students to consider could include:

  • Continuity and change – growth of industrialisation and movement of people domestically and globally
  • Cause and effect – the Great Depression, the interwar period and the rise of political ideologies
  • Perspectives – changing views about the rights and freedoms of enslaved peoples
  • Significance – revolutions in France, America and Russia
  • Contestability – controversies over innovations such as steam power, electricity and development and use of weapons, including the atomic bomb.

Historical skills

Suggested applications of historical skills for students to integrate with content could include:

  • creating an annotated timeline of the key events from the Industrial Revolution to the Second World War highlighting the interconnectedness of events
  • comparing and contrasting sources from the American and French Revolutions to understand the influence of the key ideas underpinning these revolutions
  • researching how the emergence of nation-states transformed political landscapes, fostered nationalism and fuelled conflicts
  • composing a speech on the rise of nation-states considering both the advantages and disadvantages for people and governance
  • analysing political cartoons from the era of the Paris Peace Conference and explain how WWI changed the world
  • creating a presentation to demonstrate the link between the Great Depression and WWII.

Inquiry questions

Suggested questions for students to consider when planning a historical inquiry:

  • How did the Industrial Revolution transform living and working conditions?
  • What were the experiences of immigrants and enslaved peoples during the 19th and early 20th centuries?
  • How did the American and French Revolutions shape ideas about human rights and governance?
  • What is the link between imperialism and the outbreak of WWI?
  • What were the geopolitical consequences of the decisions made during the Paris Peace Conference?
  • How did economic, social and political factors contribute to the rise of ideologies such as fascism, nationalism and communism in this period?

Suggested case and site studies

Case studies and site studies are an opportunity to extend students’ knowledge and understanding and to actively participate in historical inquiry. Site studies can be in person or virtual and should be accessible to all students.

Suggested case studiesSuggested site studies
  • Jack Lang and the opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge
  • The American Civil War and abolition of slavery
  • The formation of the League of Nations
  • Revolutions in Russia
  • Ironbridge Gorge, England
  • Karl Marx’s tomb, Highgate Cemetery, England
  • Ellis Island, New York, USA
  • Museums of History NSW (MHNSW), Sydney
  • Versailles Palace, France

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing guidance for students to create written texts using scaffolds and exemplars.
  • Providing opportunities for explicit reading comprehension and vocabulary development that are relevant to this focus area.
  • Providing opportunities for students to apply numeracy to interpret historical events.
  • Selecting source material considering the readability levels of written material, availability of audio transcripts, closed captions with videos or tactile replicas of maps or objects. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access sources and information.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic support where appropriate and use their home language or dialect when using sources and planning writing.
  • Extending students by encouraging them to analyse how major political and social transformation in this period reshaped global relationships and contributed to the modern world.
